concepts.title: A payout isn’t all profit.
concepts.rationale: A branching money diagram separates the headline payout into the original stake and actual profit. The two pockets make a common odds-reading distinction visible at a glance.
concepts.caption: That payout includes some money you already put in. Example: a $10 bet at +150 returns $25 if it wins — $10 stake back, plus $15 profit. If it loses, the $10 stake is lost. Separate the stake from the profit when you read the numbers.
concepts.alt: Playbook sports math card on navy. Headline: A payout isn’t all profit. Example: a $10 bet at +150 odds. A diagram branches from $25, total back if your bet wins, into $10, your stake back, and +$15, your profit. Text: The payout includes the money you put in. If the bet loses, it’s gone. Action: Separate the stake from the profit. A protected footer displays free support and age information from the brand configuration.

sources.note: The +150 definition gives $150 profit per $100 stake. Scaling by one tenth gives $15 profit on $10. Adding the returned $10 stake gives $25 total return; both the stake and odds are visible on the card.
Under How it works, an incorrect bet loses the stake. The card states this alongside the winning-return example.

concepts.title: “Almost” isn’t a forecast.
concepts.rationale: A near-miss display becomes an interrupted prediction arrow. The weather-forecast hook gives the myth a memorable label without mocking the player or suggesting a technique for winning.
concepts.caption: Two matching symbols can feel like a hint. They aren’t a forecast. A near miss doesn’t make the next slot spin more likely to win: each spin is independent. Share the fact next time “almost” lands.

A crossed arrow accompanies No preview of the next spin. Text: A near miss doesn’t make the next spin more likely to win. Each spin is independent. Action: Share this next time “almost” lands. sources.section: Myth 4: Near Misses Mean You're Close
sources.note: The article and quiz explain that near misses carry no predictive information and that the next spin is independent. The artwork explicitly labels its invented reel combination a non-winning illustration rather than claiming a universal paytable rule.
Tip 5 states that previous spin results do not affect the next spin. No numerical probability is inferred from the pictured symbols.

concepts.title: Read the × before the $.
concepts.rationale: The multiplication sign takes top billing over a promotional dollar figure. A large equation exposes the wagering requirement, followed by two concrete terms to check.
concepts.caption: A bonus has more than one number. Example: a $50 bonus with a 20× rule on the bonus alone means $1,000 in qualifying bets before bonus withdrawal. Check which games count and when the offer expires. Read the terms before opting in.
concepts.alt: Playbook bonus decoder card on emerald. Headline: Read the × before the $. The stated example is a 20-times wagering rule that applies to the bonus only. A navy equation panel reads $50 bonus multiplied by 20 multiplier equals $1,000 in qualifying bets required before bonus withdrawal. Text: Check which games count and when the offer expires. Action: Read the terms before opting in. A protected navy footer displays free support and age information from the brand configuration.

sources.section: Myth 20: A Bonus Is Free Money
sources.note: The entry defines wagering requirements as a multiplier applied to the bonus and discusses game restrictions and expiry. This original example uses $50 × 20 = $1,000 in qualifying bets. The bonus-only basis is explicitly stated on the card; no expected-loss or withdrawal guarantee is claimed.
RC-9 supports reading the full terms before opting in.

notes: Illustrative English comparison masters, not operator-specific offers or active controls. Bonus rules and eligible game contributions vary; the example specifies a bonus-only multiplier and qualifying bets. Slot artwork is an invented non-winning example, not a universal paytable. Support and age placeholders resolve from the common brand configuration, and need the intended operator/jurisdiction configuration before public use. All claims use the common packet and simple arithmetic; no external research or raster image assets were used.
